title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

claims.text: Reading from the data lake is the dominant I/O cost for warehouse queries, so the engine layers local caches (memory and SSD) over remote storage to cut the number of remote reads.

Caching in the warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint is fully transparent and always on: queries cache whatever data they touch regardless of origin, including warehouse tables, OneLake shortcuts, and even shortcuts that point at non-Azure storage.

On first access the engine transcodes data from its file-based format into a compressed columnar in-memory representation; storing each column's values together improves compression and lets operations on one column avoid touching the others.
The columnar in-memory cache layout enables parallel execution across columns, so the engine can exploit multi-core processors when scanning, filtering, and aggregating large datasets.
Anything loaded into the in-memory cache is also serialized to a local SSD disk cache, which acts as a larger second tier for datasets that exceed memory capacity.

Because the SSD cache is larger than the in-memory cache, data evicted from memory typically survives on SSD; rehydrating memory from the SSD cache is much faster than refetching from remote storage, smoothing out query performance.
Cache eviction is recency-based: when the cache hits its capacity threshold while new data is read in, the objects unused for the longest time are removed first.
The cache maintains full transactional consistency: DML changes to data in storage after it was cached still yield consistent query results.

Users cannot disable, configure, or manually clear the warehouse caches; Microsoft Fabric orchestrates cache management entirely, and Microsoft notes disabling it would visibly degrade query performance.
In-memory and disk caching are distinct from result set caching, which is a separate warehouse feature: the former cache the data being scanned, the latter caches completed query results.
